extracted.intended_audience: students, practitioners, and general readers interested in U.S. administrative law and Supreme Court deference doctrines
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the standards and factual tests from Skidmore v. Swift & Co. for (1) how much judicial deference to give agency interpretations and (2) how to determine whether on-call/waiting time counts as working time under the FLSA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore deference (persuasiveness-based deference)
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative agency's interpretative rules deserve deference according to their persuasiveness; the Court adopted a case-by-case test (Skidmore deference) which considers the rulings, interpretations, and opinions of the administrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court stated that such rulings, interpretations and opinions 'while not controlling upon the courts by reason of their authority, do constitute a body of experience and informed judgment to which courts and litigants may properly resort for guidance.' Deference under Skidmore is not automatic or controlling but rests on the persuasive power of the agency's position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore deference factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to determine how persuasive an agency interpretation is (the elements the Court used to measure Skidmore deference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court developed a test considering: (1) 'The thoroughness of the agency's investigation'; (2) 'The validity of its reasoning'; (3) 'The consistency of its interpretation over time'; and (4) 'Other persuasive powers of the agency.' These elements guide a court's assessment of how much weight to give an agency's non-binding interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrator's interpretative bulletins as guidance (example: Wage and Hour Bulletin No. 13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency interpretative bulletins and similar publications can provide a guide on how to settle disputes about statutory application under particular circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion cites the Administrator's Bulletin No. 13 as providing 'standards and examples to guide in particular situations.' The Court emphasized the Administrator's accumulated experience in resolving problems (e.g., ascertaining working time in employment involving periods of inactivity) and that such views can be relied upon for guidance even if not controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether waiting/on-call time counts as working time — factual inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of whether waiting or on-call time falls within the FLSA's working time is a question of fact to be resolved by trial courts; the Court did not lay down a rigid legal formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court stated: 'Whether waiting time falls within or without the Act is a question of fact, to be resolved by the trial courts.' The decision reversed and remanded for further proceedings to allow the factual record to determine the status of on-call time.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-call time assessment criteria (degree of freedom and consecutive hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical test for calculating working time during periods of idleness while an employee is subject to call.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court quoted that the calculation depends 'upon the degree to which the employee is free to engage in personal activities during periods of idleness when he is subject to call and the number of consecutive hours that the employee is subject to call without being required to perform active work.' The opinion applies this: sleeping and eating time may be excluded if the employees were 'very rarely interrupted' and these pursuits are of a 'purely private nature,' while other on-call time may be included if evidence shows the time was not spent as the employees would have chosen if free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between formal and informal agency documents for deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Different types of agency materials may attract different levels of judicial deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As explained in later cases cited on the page (e.g., Christensen v. Harris County), formal agency documents (such as legislative rules) are treated differently from less formal ones (such as opinion letters). Informal papers typically do not receive Chevron-style deference but are entitled to Skidmore (persuasiveness-based) deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron two-step test (summary of alternative deference framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: A later, influential framework (Chevron) for judicial review that contrasts with Skidmore by giving controlling deference when statutory ambiguity and a permissible agency construction exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chevron's two-step analysis: (1) determine whether Congress has directly spoken to the precise question; if Congress's intent is clear, give effect to it; (2) if the statute is silent or ambiguous, determine whether the agency's answer is based on a permissible construction of the statute. (Page notes Chevron later became dominant until it was overturned by Loper Bright, but Skidmore remained as a basis for deference where agency action lacks force of law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: United States v. Mead formulation reinforcing Skidmore
rubrics_metrics.description: Mead explicitly reaffirms Skidmore and articulates related factors for deference where agency interpretations lack statutory rulemaking authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mead reiterates that deference for such agency interpretations depends on 'the agency's care, its consistency, formality, and relative expertness, and to the persuasiveness of the agency's position.' This wording supplements Skidmore's factors and is cited as a controlling approach for non-rulemaking agency materials.
